cells.tense: Right now, you're tending things and it's working.
cells.verb: keeping more than one thing alive at once, with a steady hand
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why
cells.ask: If you want it: let one thing you've tended be seen finished — tell someone what it took, and then set it down. What comes back is tending that doesn't wear you out: holding what grows without gripping it.
cells.core:
Right now, you're tending things and it's working. There's more than one thing that needs you, and you aren't choosing between them — you're keeping both alive, and you know which one needs you today without having to work it out. Nothing's being forced. The care goes where it's needed and the rest gets left alone, and that's not luck. That's you reading the room correctly.

If you want to take it somewhere: let one thing you've tended be seen finished. Tell someone what it cost you, and then let it go. Not because you're done caring — because it's done, and completion is allowed to feel like completion. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without having to hold on to it.
cells.sheetLine: You know what needs you today, and you're giving it that — no more.

cells.verb: checking and adjusting and managing what's growing before it's had a chance to grow
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why
cells.ask: Pick one thing that already came good and sit with it finished — let yourself feel how it turned out before you go fix anything else. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it.
cells.core:
You're already tending tomorrow's problems. Somewhere ahead there's a version of this where something you're responsible for goes wrong because you looked away, and you're living in that version — so you check, adjust, rebalance, make sure. Both things get your attention all the time. Neither gets the room it needs to grow on its own. And the part of you that knows what matters is being drowned out by the part that's trying to cover everything.

Here's an offer: pick one thing you tended that already turned out well. Sit with it finished. Let yourself actually feel how it came good before you go fix anything else. The satisfaction isn't a reward for the tending — it's the thing that tells you when to stop. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending so hard nothing gets to grow.

cells.tense: The tending has stopped, and you're still standing where you set it down.
cells.verb: letting what needs care go uncared for
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why
cells.ask: Pick one hope you set down and keep showing up for it — not fixing, just returning. Energy into still wanting it pulls the tending back through. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it.
cells.core:
The tending has stopped, and you're still standing where you set it down. You know what matters — you can feel it, if you're honest — but the care is sitting behind you instead of in your hands, and the door you're facing is one that's already closed. The knowing didn't leave. The hands did. Now there's more than one thing that needs you and you're not quite reaching either.

Don't try to force the care back. That's the empty place, and pushing on it doesn't fill it. Instead: pick one hope you put down and keep showing up for it — not fixing, not managing, just returning to it, whatever's happened since. Still wanting it is the fuel. The tending comes back on its own once there's something you're still hoping for. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it.
cells.sheetLine: You know what needs you. You stopped showing up for it.

cells.tense: You're already keeping two things alive at once, and you'd tell anyone it just works out.
cells.verb: quietly tending what grows, and keeping more than one thing in balance
cells.place: in the part of you that knows what matters before you can say why
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, what you've been keeping alive and what it's cost you. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it, and knowing it's you doing the holding.
cells.core:
You're already keeping two things alive at once, and you'd tell anyone it just works out. It doesn't just work out. You're reading what each one needs and giving it that, day after day, without making a fuss — and because there's no fuss, you've stopped counting it as something you do. The knowing is yours. The tending is yours. The story you tell is that things take care of themselves around you.

Here's the simplest version: say out loud, to one person, what you've been keeping alive and what it's taken from you. Not for credit — so the care has a name and an owner. What comes back is care that doesn't exhaust you: holding what grows without clutching it, and knowing it's you doing the holding.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending this. You just call it luck.
